question: What is the primary site of absorption for most orally administered medications?
explanation: The extensive surface area and rich blood supply of the small intestine make it the primary site where oral drugs pass into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do certain medications require a higher dosage when given orally than intravenously?

options.A: Hepatic first-pass metabolism reduces the active drug concentration
options.B: Intestinal flora actively synthesizes antagonists against the drug
options.C: Gastric acid completely destroys all active chemical compounds
options.D: Renal clearance accelerates immediately following oral ingestion

explanation: The liver metabolizes a fraction of the drug before it reaches general circulation, which lowers its overall bioavailability. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary advantage of the oral route of drug administration?
explanation: Oral medications allow patients to manage their own therapeutic regimens easily outside of clinical settings. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h2)

question: What makes the oral route unsuitable for treating acute, life-threatening emergencies?

options.A: Patients in crises refuse to swallow liquids
options.B: Emergency drugs are chemically unstable in water
options.C: Intravenous equipment is legally required first
options.D: The onset of therapeutic action is too slow

explanation: Because absorption takes time and first-pass metabolism occurs, oral drugs cannot provide the rapid plasma levels needed in acute crises. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h2)

question: What action must a nurse take before pouring a liquid medication that is a suspension?

options.D: Warm the container in hot water

explanation: Suspensions settle over time, so shaking ensures the active pharmaceutical ingredient is evenly distributed in the liquid. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why are certain tablets manufactured with an enteric coating?

options.A: To speed up the immediate absorption of the drug in the oral cavity
options.B: To prevent the drug from dissolving in the acidic environment of the stomach
options.C: To mask an intensely bitter taste for pediatric populations
options.D: To combine two incompatible chemical compounds into one pill

explanation: Enteric coatings protect drugs that irritate the gastric mucosa or get destroyed by stomach acid, ensuring they dissolve safely in the alkaline small intestine. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h3)

question: A patient scheduled for an oral antihypertensive is drowsy and has a weak gag reflex. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.B: Proceed with administration while sitting them upright
options.C: Crush the pill and mix it into a cup of water
options.D: Withhold the medication and notify the prescriber

explanation: Impaired consciousness and a weak gag reflex compromise swallowing safety, making oral administration a high aspiration risk. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h4)

question: How many patient identifiers should a nurse check before medication administration?
explanation: Standard safety protocols require verifying at least two unique identifiers, such as name and hospital number, to prevent administration errors. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h4)

question: When is the correct time to document that a medication has been given to a patient?

options.A: Immediately after the patient swallows the medication
options.B: As soon as the prescription is verified by pharmacy
options.C: Right before pouring the medication into the cup
options.D: At the end of the entire nursing shift

explanation: Documentation should always occur immediately after administration to prevent accidental double-dosing or missed charting. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h5)

question: A nurse notices that a medication order states an intravenous antibiotic should be given orally. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Convert the dose to a liquid suspension and give it by mouth
options.B: Hold the medication and clarify the route with the prescriber
options.C: Administer the medication orally as written on the chart
options.D: Crush the tablet and dissolve it for intravenous infusion

explanation: The nurse must verify discrepancies in routes of administration with the prescribing clinician before proceeding to prevent patient harm. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why must the nurse remain at the bedside until the patient swallows all medications?

options.A: To confirm ingestion and prevent hidden hoarding or omission
options.B: To wash the medication cup immediately after use
options.C: To measure the exact time of first-pass metabolism
options.D: To prevent the patient from drinking too much water

explanation: Staying at the bedside guarantees the patient actually takes the drugs rather than hiding them or failing to swallow them. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h6)

question: What physical body position should the nurse place the patient in before administering oral medication?
explanation: An upright sitting position uses gravity to assist swallowing and protects the airway from accidental aspiration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is a major risk when mixing a crushed pediatric medication into a staple food like milk or porridge?

options.A: The pediatric patient will absorb the medication through the oral mucosa
options.B: The mixture will instantly turn into an unabsorbable gel
options.C: The food will completely neutralize the therapeutic properties of the drug
options.D: The child may later refuse that food group entirely due to an altered taste

explanation: Associating essential nutritional foods with unpleasant medicinal tastes can cause children to reject healthy meals later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h7)

question: What measuring device should a nurse use to give liquid medications to an infant accurately?
explanation: Oral syringes provide precise milliliter measurements, preventing dangerous under-dosing or overdosing in infants. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h7)

question: What action should a nurse take if a patient refuses a scheduled oral medication?

options.A: Ignore the refusal and leave the medication on the bedside table
options.B: Crush the medication and slip it into their drinking water secretly
options.C: Document the refusal, the stated reason, and notify the prescriber
options.D: Force the patient to swallow the medication to maintain compliance

explanation: Competent patients have the right to refuse treatment; nurses must document this safely and inform the medical team. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h8)

question: Which of the following must be recorded in the patient chart immediately following medication administration?

options.A: Detailed personal history of the pharmacist
options.C: Manufacturer batch number and expiry date
options.D: Drug name, dose, route, and time given

explanation: Standard documentation requires capturing the core medication details promptly to maintain an accurate clinical record. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h8)
